content.subject: Slip and fall at the grocery store — looking for representation
content.body:
Hello,

I was referred to your firm by my friend Lorraine Pickering, who said you were thorough and easy to work with. I'm hoping you can help me with a fall I had three weeks ago.

On the evening of April 23rd, I was shopping at Crestwell Market on Shea Boulevard in Scottsdale. It was around 7:15pm. I had just turned into the dairy aisle when my right foot slid out from under me on what turned out to be a puddle of liquid — I think it was olive oil from a broken bottle on the lower shelf that hadn't been cleaned up. There was no wet floor sign, no caution cone, nothing. I went down hard on my left hip and my right wrist took most of the impact when I tried to catch myself.

A store employee named Devon (I didn't get a last name, but he was wearing a name tag and a green apron) came over within about thirty seconds. He was apologetic and said something like, 'Oh no, I saw that bottle earlier and was supposed to come back to it.' He helped me to a bench near the customer service desk and called the manager, a woman named Patrice Holloway. She filled out an incident report and gave me a copy. The report number is CM-INC-2026-0419-A.

I declined the ambulance they offered because I was conscious and could move, but my daughter Imogen drove me to HonorHealth Shea Emergency Department about an hour later when the wrist swelling got worse. X-rays showed a distal radius fracture and a deep hip contusion. They put me in a wrist splint, gave me crutches because the hip was making weight-bearing difficult, and referred me to an orthopedist, Dr. Yusuf Calderwood at Camelback Orthopedic Associates. I saw Dr. Calderwood the following Monday and he confirmed the fracture was non-displaced but recommended I wear the splint for six weeks. I've been doing prescribed exercises and I have a follow-up next Tuesday.

I'm 64 years old and I work part-time as a bookkeeper for Whitfield & Sons Roofing — about 22 hours a week. I've been able to work from home since the fall, so I haven't lost income, but I can't lift my grandson Theo (he's two) and I've had to cancel a trip to Coeur d'Alene to see my sister that we'd been planning since January. I'm also right-handed, which has made everything from cooking to brushing my teeth take twice as long.

The store manager called me twice in the first week to check in, which I appreciated. The second time, she mentioned their 'claims department' would be in touch. A man named Reginald Astor from Crestwell's risk management group called me on May 6th and asked if I'd be willing to discuss 'resolving the matter directly.' I told him I needed to think about it and hung up. He called again on May 12th. I haven't returned his second call.

My medical bills so far are about $4,200 (ER copay, ortho visits, the splint, two follow-up X-rays). My health insurance through Blue Mesa is covering the rest but I know they'll want to be paid back if I recover anything.

What I have: the incident report copy, photos my daughter took of the spill area before they cleaned it up (she went back into the aisle while I was on the bench — smart girl), the ER discharge paperwork, Dr. Calderwood's notes, and a folder of receipts. I'd be happy to come in and bring all of it.

A few questions while I'm thinking of them: Do I need to file something with the store formally, or does that happen through you? Should I keep talking to Mr. Astor or stop entirely? And how long does something like this usually take?

Let me know what you need from me. Afternoons work best — I'm usually free after 2pm.

Thank you,
Bernadette Thrushwood
(480) 555-0173
